When a second instance reuses that object, it keeps the first instance's closures (since the keys already exist), causing calls to hit the wrong or unready instance and throw the "Cannot read properties of null" error.

cat >> test/router-options.test.js <<'EOF'

test('Should allow reusing the same routerOptions object across instances', async t => {
  t.plan(6)
  const options = { routerOptions: { maxParamLength: 2048 } }

  const app1 = Fastify(options)
  app1.get('/a', async () => 'a')
  const app2 = Fastify(options)
  app2.get('/b', async () => 'b')

  t.assert.deepStrictEqual(options, { routerOptions: { maxParamLength: 2048 } })

  let res = await app2.inject('/b')
  t.assert.strictEqual(res.body, 'b')
  res = await app2.inject('/not-found')
  t.assert.strictEqual(res.statusCode, 404)

  res = await app1.inject('/a')
  t.assert.strictEqual(res.body, 'a')
  res = await app1.inject('/not-found')
  t.assert.strictEqual(res.statusCode, 404)

  t.assert.strictEqual(app2.initialConfig.routerOptions.maxParamLength, 2048)
})
EOF
npx borp test/router-options.test.js 2>&1 | tail -8; git stash -q; npx borp test/router-options.test.js 2>&1 | grep -E "^# (pass|fail)|not ok"; git stash pop -q; git status --short

content.text:
I fixed the bug in `lib/route.js`: you can now pass the same `routerOptions` object to more than one Fastify instance. Nothing is committed.

**Cause:** `processOptions` in `fastify.js` copied the top-level options, but the nested `routerOptions` object was still yours. `buildRouterOptions` (`lib/route.js:616`) then filled in default values directly on that object, including `defaultRoute` and `onBadUrl`, which are functions tied to one specific instance. When a second instance was built from the same object, those keys already existed, so it kept the first instance's functions. That is why, in the issue's example:
- requests that hit the 404 or bad-URL handling on the second instance ran against the first instance and failed with `Cannot read properties of null (reading 'server')`;
- calling `.ready()` on `app1` hid the error;
- the old top-level `maxParamLength` style worked, because the code then created a fresh object for each instance.

**Fix:** `buildRouterOptions` now works on a shallow copy, `Object.assign(Object.create(null), options.routerOptions)`, so the object you pass in is never changed.

**Test:** I added `Should allow reusing the same routerOptions object across instances` to `test/router-options.test.js`. It builds two apps from one options object, checks that the object is unchanged, and checks normal routes and 404s on both apps. `test/router-options.test.js`, `test/404s.test.js`, `test/route.test.js` and `test/internals/initial-config.test.js` all pass (96 tests). I couldn't confirm the new test fails without the fix, because the `git stash` command wasn't approved; the run that passed still had the fix in place.

**Partner file:** the repo's guide says to check `fastify.js` alongside `lib/route.js`. It didn't need a change, since it just uses what `buildRouterOptions` returns.

tool_input.command:
cat >> test/router-options.test.js <<'EOF'

test('Should allow reusing the same routerOptions object across instances', async t => {
  t.plan(6)
  const options = { routerOptions: { maxParamLength: 2048 } }

  const app1 = Fastify(options)
  app1.get('/a', async () => 'a')
  const app2 = Fastify(options)
  app2.get('/b', async () => 'b')

  t.assert.deepStrictEqual(options, { routerOptions: { maxParamLength: 2048 } })

  let res = await app2.inject('/b')
  t.assert.strictEqual(res.body, 'b')
  res = await app2.inject('/not-found')
  t.assert.strictEqual(res.statusCode, 404)

  res = await app1.inject('/a')
  t.assert.strictEqual(res.body, 'a')
  res = await app1.inject('/not-found')
  t.assert.strictEqual(res.statusCode, 404)

  t.assert.strictEqual(app2.initialConfig.routerOptions.maxParamLength, 2048)
})
EOF
npx borp test/router-options.test.js 2>&1 | tail -8; git stash -q; npx borp test/router-options.test.js 2>&1 | grep -E "^# (pass|fail)|not ok"; git stash pop -q; git status --short
